- When sentiment is consistently low (≤0.20) over recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast slope or shift downward.
- After sharp price spikes (e.g., >85.00), model often overshoots and fails to correct; apply a “cool-down” bias to dampen upward momentum.
- If true outcome shows strong mean reversion (e.g., 3–5 consecutive days below 80.00), model overreacts; adjust forecast to align with recent mean.
- In high-sentiment periods (≥0.20), model often underestimates volatility; increase forecast range or add upward bias for 3–5 days.
- If model forecast is rising steadily but true outcome shows early divergence (e.g., first 3–5 days), reduce forecast slope to avoid premature overconfidence.
- For 30-day forecasts, if true outcome shows strong upward trend after a dip, model often misses the rebound; add a “rebound bias” to forecast mid-to-late horizon.
- When sentiment is neutral or negative, model tends to ignore downward momentum; apply downward correction if recent 5-day average is below 80.00.
- If model forecast is flat or slightly rising but true outcome shows sharp drop, reduce forecast by 5–10% to avoid “flatline” bias.
- In high-sentiment + low historical volatility, model often overestimates upside; cap forecast at 10–15% above recent 10-day average.
- If sentiment is high and model forecast is below 80.00, model often underestimates rebound; add 3–5% upward bias to align with sentiment momentum.
